case_source: in the matter of an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908  for setting aside the order dt. 6-1-75 and 15.1.75 of the Munsif, 2nd Court Satkhira, Khulna passed in Misc. case No. 235/73, 244/73.
full_judgment:
These two Rules are directed against two orders of the learned Munsif in two different proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Munsif rejected the application for addition of parties in each of the proceedings.

2. One Ruhul Amin Sardar filed an application under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for correction of record of right in respect of the properties mentioned in the schedule to the application. It is Khatian No. 2184 Plot No. 2594 measuring 11.97 acres. This land has been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 in the name of the Deputy Commissioner. In this application Bangladesh has been impleaded as opposite party No. 1 and Sailuddin Sardar, Golam Rabbani and Ramjan Ali, the three brothers of Ruhul Amin have been impleaded as opposite parties 2 to 4 (preform) The allegations made in the petition are that the land in question originally belonged to Roy Harendra Nath and others in khas under the anent-merit and the petitioner Ruhul Amin and his three other brothers took settlement of Plot No. 2594 at a rental of Rs 90-8 annas in 1332 B S. and continued to possess the same along with other lands. The said lands have been wrongly recorded in the impugned current khatian.

Prayers have been made in the following terms:

(ক) ছায়েলের আরজির বর্ণনামতে তফসিল বর্ণিত ১১০৯৭ শতাংশ জমিতে ছায়েলের আরজির বর্ণিত রায়তি জমার স্বত্য প্রকাশ হয়।

(খ) দাবীকৃত জমি সম্পর্কে Record ছায়েলের বিরুদ্ধে বাধ্যকর না থাকা প্রকাশ হয়।

(গ) দাবীকৃত জমি সম্পর্কে Co (Rev.) সাহেবের Report দৃষ্টে ছায়েলেরকে ডিগ্রি দিতে মর্জি হয়।

(ঘ) বর্তমান মকদ্দমার যাবতীয় খরচ ছায়েলখান।

(ঙ) যুক্তি মতে ছায়েল আর যে কোন প্রতিকার চান তাহাও পান।

On this application Miscellaneous case No 235 of 1973 (143A) was started.

3. Sailuddin Sardar Golam Rabbani and Ramjan Ali as petitioners filed a similar petition under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on the allegations inter alia that they have tenancy in respect of 12.71 acres of land which has been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 in the name of Deputy Commissioner. Reliefs have been prayed in the same terms as in the case of Ruhul Amin Sardar. In this case Bangladesh has been impeladed as opposite party No. 1 and Ruhul Amin has been impleaded as opposite party No. 2 (proforma) and on this application Miscellaneous case No. 244 of 1973 (143) was started.

4. The Bangladesh appeared in both the cases and filed written objection. Thereafter the order sheets indicates various other developments of the proceedings. Upon application of the instant petitioners for addition of parties under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned Munsif heard the parties and rejected the application in both the cases. According to the learned Munsif, the application was not maintainable and Tenancy Act does not provide for addition of opposite parties. Against the aforesaid order of the learned Munsif the instant Rules were obtained. It appears that an order has been recorded for analogous bearing of, the two Rules. Accordingly, both the Rules are taken up together for bearing.

5. Mr. A.F.M. Shahid, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rules has contended that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in rejecting the prayer for addition of parties. According to the learned Advocate, Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was applicable and the learned Munsif acted illegally in the exercise of jurisdiction in holding that the petition was not maintainable. Mr. Shahid submits that section 143A contemplated a civil proceeding and as such section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies. Since no provision has been specifically made in section 143A for addition of opposite parties, according to Mr. Shahid, Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is the appropriate provision enabling the applicants to seek the remedy prayed for.

6. Mr. M.B. Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties in both the Rules, contends that section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Order I rule 10 have no application in the special provisions for correction of record of right under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. According to Mr. Rahman the applications for addition of parties are misconceived and not maintainable. It is, therefore, necessary to consider what section 143A stands for. It runs as follows:

"(1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites, for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record of rights in the Civil Court which would have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made.

(2) An application filed under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be a plaint and order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

(3) An application filed under sub-section (1) shall contain full particulars of persons likely to be affected by an order on such application and shall also contain the full particulars of the holding to which the entry relates or in respect of which the omission complained of was made.

(4) The Court shall, for the purpose of disposal of application filed under sub-section (1), follow the following procedure, namely :

(a) the Court shall reuse notice to be served on the persons named in the application in the manner as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

(b) the Court shall, within seven days of the filing of an application under sub-section (I), send a copy thereof by registered post at the applicant's cost to the Revenue Officer concerned for holding a local inquiry, in presence of the parties concerned, on the subject-matter of the application and the Revenue Officer shall within fifteen days of the receipt of the copy, hold inquiry and submit the report to the Court.

(c) the Court may allow such reasonable time as it may think fit to file objection to the inquiry report referred to in clause

(b) and, if no appearance is made by the opposite party within the time mentioned in notice, and, if no objection is filed to the inquiry report within the time so allowed, the court may proceed ex-parte with disposal of the application after taking into consideration the said report and other material evidence on record, and

(d) where the report referred to in clause (b) is not submitted, or where objection referred to in clause (c) is filed, the Court shall fix a date for hearing and on that date after hearing the parties and taking into consideration the report, if any, and other evidence which may be adduced by the parties in this behalf, shall pass such order as it may think just and proper.

(5) Any person whose interest has been affected by reason of an entry or omission in the record-of-rights, referred to in sub-section (1), may within fourteen days of the filing of an application under sub-section (1), appear to be added as co-applicant.

(6) The Revenue Officer shall, for the purpose of an inquiry under sub-section (4), have the same power as vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including the power of:-

(a) enforcing attendance of any person, and examining him on oath, and

(b) compelling the production of any document.

(7) Within thirty days from the date of an order under sub-section (4), an appeal from that order shall lie to the District Judge who may, either himself bear the appeal or transfer it to any other court subordinate to him but not below the rank of a Subordinate Judge for hearing.

(8) Decision under sub-section (4), if no appeal is preferred from it, or under sub-section (7), shall be final and conclusive.

(9) Where the Court passes an order under sub-section (4) or sub section (7) revising the 	entries or rectifying the omission complained of under sub-section (1), it shall notify the same to the Collector and the Collector shall correct the record of rights accordingly.

(10) Any person interested may produce a certified copy of the orders referred to in sub-section (4) or sub-section (7) to the Revenue Officer and the Revenue Officer shall make such alterations in the record of rights as may be necessary to give effect to such orders.

(11) The record of rights corrected under sub-section (9) or subsection (10) shall be deemed to have been prepared and finally published under chapter IV of this Act.

(12) An application under subsection (1) or memorandum of an appeal under sub-section 	(7) shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the Court Fees Act, 1870, bear a fixed court fee of rupee one.

(13) For the purpose of an application, appeal, review, revision and consequence of 	nonappearance, relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall mutatis mutandis apply".

7. Mr. Shahid has referred to sub-section (21 which according to him makes the proceeding a suit since the application is to "be deemed to be a plaint and the order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure". Accordingly, he contends that section 143A contemplates a decree and the proceeding is to be deemed to be a suit. That being so, his further contention is that section 141 and Order / rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure have application in proceeding under section 143A, Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows :

"The procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction".

Rule, 10, Order I reads as follows:-

"Where a suit has been instituted in the name of the wrong person as plaintiff or where it is doubtful whether it has been instituted in the name of the right plaintiff, the Court may at any stage of the suit, if satisfied that the suit has been instituted through a bonafide mistake, and that it is necessary for the determination of the real matter in dispute so to do, order any other person to be substituted or added as plaintiff upon such terms as the court thinks just.

(2) The Court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the Court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to ad-judicator upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit be added.

(3) No person shall be added as a plaintiff suing without a next friend or as the next friend of a plaintiff under any disability without his consent.

(4) Where a defendant is added, the plaint shall unless the court otherwise directs, be amended in such manner as may be, necessary, and amended copies of the summons and of the plaint shall be served on the new defendant and, if the court thinks fit, on the original defendant.

(5) Subject to the provisions of the Indian Limitation Act, 1877, section 22, the proceedings as against any person added as defendant shall be deemed to have been only on the service of the summons".

<u>8. Assuming, as Mr. Shahid contends, that in the instant proceeding Order 1 rule 10 shall apply, evidently, sub-rule (1) has no manner of application. In terms of sub-rule (2) the court jurisdiction to add a party whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all questions involved in the suit. In the background of the above provision, can it be said that section 143A contemplates a proceeding of such nature or is a proceeding which is deemed to be a suit where all questions involved in the suit or proceeding may be effectually and completely adjudicated upon ? Obviously section 143A contemplates a summary power to be exercised by the Civil Court within the prescribed limits. The purpose of introducing this special provision is "correcting mistakes". The special provisions made in section 143A are intended for a definite and limited purpose. The legislative intent is clearly available from the language used in sub-section (I) of section 143A. Sub-section (2) contains the statutory fiction for extending the meaning of the terms "application" and "order" which they do not in reality imply but the statute requires them to be as such. Sub-section (2) does not enlarge the scope, object and purpose of sub-section (1). The procedure prescribed in the subsequent sub-sections is intended for the purpose of carrying out the purpose and object of "correcting mistakes". Sub-section (13) indicates that relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall mutatis mutandis apply for the purpose of an application, appeal, review, revision and consequence of non-appearance. It is difficult to conceive that the Code of Civil Procedure has been made applicable in its terms and as a whole. Therefore, the contention of Mr. Shahid that section 143A. not bring exhaustive and in the absence of provision for addition of opposite parties there in, the provisions of Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall apply on the strength of section 141 of the Code does not appear to stand on a sound footing within the meaning and scope of, section 143A of the State Acquit sit ion and Tenancy Act. Thus, the application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. does not appeal to be maintainable. The learned Munsif in this behalf appears to have rightly rejected the petition for addition of parties.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Shahid has next contended that the applicants are some of the members of the public and they came to protect a public right in the nature of easement in respect of the suit land. The scope of enquiry under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act relates to correcting mistakes in respect of an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, the right of the applicants, if any, cannot be adjudicated in the instant proceeding. The applicants not being parties can never be affected by an order passed in the proceeding. According to Mr. Shahid the members of the public have been enjoying a right recognised by the Government. It does not appear that the Government has denied the right of the public The alleged right of easement is sought to be confirmed by the applicants In the instant proceeding but this question is absolutely beyond the scope of investigation under section 143A.</u>

10. Mr. Shahid has finally contended that the addition of parties is necessary for avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. This is being the question. Since section 143A does not permit adjudication of the alleged right of easement, there is no question of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings.

<u>11. It must, however, be pointed out that section 143A is not intended to be misused in the way it has been sought to be done in the instant applications. In paragraph 5 of the respective petition, certain prayers have been made in declaratory form with regard to title of the petitioner or petitioners. It does not appear that section 143A contemplates such a relief as prayed for in the two cases. It further appears that the trial court proceeded to deal with the two cases as if these are suits for title. It appears that an Advocate Commissioner was appointed and he submitted certain report. Could the question, be decided within the scope of section 143A. The reply evidently is in the negative. Caution should be taken by the Court below not to encourage adjudication of disputed title and possession under the garb of a proceeding under section 143A. A complete end effectual adjudication with regard to title and possession must be left open for properly constituted suit. A proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act should not be allowed to transcend its limited scope expressly provided by statute itself. The legislative intent and purpose should not be overlooked. It is not necessary for me to express my views on the applications under section 143A, since they have to be disposed of by the trial court according to law. The observation made by me are meant for guidance of the learned Muncie who is however free to dispose of the matters on consideration of necessary questions and according to law.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above there is no ground for interference under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

The result, therefore, is that the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
